Research projects are at the heart of what most marine biologists do, whether it be actually collecting specimens in the field, compiling research data, finding real life applications for the research data, or classroom teaching.

What does a Marine Biologist do? Some of the possible careers for a marine biology graduate would include teaching at a high school or college level, being a research scientist, an oceanographic laboratory technician, working for an aquarium or zoo, or any number of possibilities for consulting with different government agencies and universities.

Another potential career for a marine biology graduate would be to become a hydrologist, which is a scientist or researcher that studies bodies of water and helps to find ways to eliminate water pollution.

There are actually many environmental careers that can be attained with a degree in marine biology. Even a fish and game warden, which is something akin to an environmental police officer, is a possible career move for a marine biology graduate.

Marine biotechnology, one of the possible specializations, involves developing and testing new drug treatments and protocols that are derived from ocean life. Another specialization is molecular biology, which is helpful in identifying microorganisms as well as diagnosing diseases that are caused by microorganisms.

How to Become a Marine Biologist? This is a field where educational requirements tend to be fairly cut and dry. A scant few entry level positions may be available for graduates with a bachelor's degree in one of the biological sciences, but the grand majority of research positions will require at least a master's degree in marine biology.

Those who wish to work their way into a position of authority where they are directing research projects will most likely need to earn a doctorate in marine biology. In other words, if you want to do your own work, rather than someone else's, you'll need a Ph.D.

Interestingly, many working marine biologists recommend that someone interested in a career in marine biology get a degree in a different biological science first and specialize in marine biology for their post-graduate work.

Specialization in a particular discipline is considered a key turning point in the career of a marine biology graduate.

What is the workplace of a Marine Biologist like? Oceanography centres, laboratories, aquariums, research boats and vessels are some of the possibilities for field workplaces.

It would not be unusual to find a marine biology graduate working in a tide pool, a swamp, a mangrove forest, a coral reef, or any place on earth that supports marine life.

Travel to interesting places is one of the possible perks for a career in marine biology. Laboratory work could involve working directly with the federal government, or the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), or on behalf of a university's research program.

Virtually every body of salt water on the planet is being studied by marine biologists, from the Caribbean seas to the arctic ocean.

Nonprofit organizations are also a major employer for marine biology graduates since they fund studies and research projects for commercial products. Drug companies conduct marine research as well, as marine life is often at the cutting edge of research.

Lovecraft also really did not like romance. Feminine women and heroic masculine men rescuing them and making families was something he despised. I've always found Lovecraft's stance on romance peculiar, but I think as someone who was ultimately a nihilist it makes sense that he would view it in the fashion he does.

As to Howard and Burroughs, they are my favorites.

Howard was ultimately distrustful of large scale civilization as something that was inherently decadent and self defeating. He viewed civilization as removing man from nature and thus cultivating the worst of his excesses. Note the stark contrasts he always draws between "barbarians" and "civilized men", he almost always portrays the barbarian as inherently honest in a fashion the civilized man isn't. Interesting that he also distinguished barbarians from "savages". I think an underlying theme of his works (at least the Conan and Kull stories) is that civilization is a temporary imposition on the natural state of the world, one destined to fail by it's own machinations but also at the mercy of a larger universe that is wholly indifferent to it.

Burroughs is an even more interesting study. Despite being from Chicago and the son of a Union soldier in many ways his John Carter stories are vehicles for exploring the morality and values of the Southern Planter Class. An honor culture where insults could be deadly serious, pseudo-chivalric values, and an emphasis on the natural place of each race as defined by its inherent characteristics.
